source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Prioritizing replay when future goals are unknown (bioRxiv preprint v. June 2025; later published in Neuron as Between planning and map building)
finding: Defines the Geodesic Representation (GR): one shortest-path Q function per candidate goal, each learned in a modified MDP where that goal is terminal and rewarding. Separates map (routes to goals) from value (which goals pay). Replay is prioritized by expected value of a Bellman backup, summed over a belief about future goals. A Dyna-SR-like agent, but goal-general.
numbers: Tabular gridworld simulations; the bottleneck example averages replay over n=250 simulations. No new animal data.
quote: it measures long-run distance from each location to each goal
limits: Tabular only; fitted qualitatively to published rodent studies, not statistically. Authors say prioritization matters only when data or compute are limited. Preprint text read, not the Neuron version.
agent_relevance: Agent memory should store routes to many likely goals, ranked by expected future need, not only the route for the current task.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Prioritizing replay when future goals are unknown (bioRxiv preprint v. June 2025; later published in Neuron as Between planning and map building)
finding: Explains the Gillespie et al. eight-arm maze result that replay lags behavior and favors the previous block's goal arm. Two Rescorla-Wagner learners: a fast one tracks the current goal for choice, a slow one estimates the goal distribution across blocks and steers replay. A Q-value replay agent (Mattar and Daw) predicts the opposite.
numbers: Rats had roughly ten blocks per goal in the whole experiment. GR agent: previous-block arm replayed most, current-arm replay rises through the block, enrichment fades over several blocks. Q agent: current arm preferred and its replay falls through the block.
limits: Qualitative match only. Relies on a small per-step forgetting decay in the map.
agent_relevance: Keep two memories on two timescales: a fast one for the current task goal and a slow one for what goals tend to come. Use the slow one to decide what to rehearse.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Prioritizing replay when future goals are unknown (bioRxiv preprint v. June 2025; later published in Neuron as Between planning and map building)
finding: Goal dynamics set whether replay lags or leads. With a known alternating goal schedule (Pfeiffer and Foster Home/Random task) GR replay is proactive toward the Home well. With a slowly learned block-level schedule it lags.
numbers: Fig 5: before Home trials, heightened Home-route replay starts right after Home is found, with no preference for the previous Random goal. Fig 6: with goal persistence p11=0.5 the GR agent replays the path to g1 then g2; with p11=0.05 it replays g2 first; the Q agent replays only the current goal at every setting.
limits: Prediction assumes the agent knows the true goal dynamics; learning those dynamics is left to future work.
agent_relevance: Order of rehearsal should depend on how long the current goal will last. Short-lived tasks mean prepare for the next task first.

source: Sagiv, Akam, Witten, Daw (2025) Prioritizing replay when future goals are unknown (bioRxiv preprint v. June 2025; later published in Neuron as Between planning and map building)
finding: Limits stated by the authors: GR is off-policy and learns routes to one goal, not sequences of goals. Fixes proposed: sets of SRs with generalized policy improvement, or hierarchy. Prioritization is defined only in tabular settings; function approximation is open.
numbers: No numbers; a limitations section.
quote: so far only well-defined in the tabular setting
limits: This is why the result has not yet been tested in deep-RL or LLM form.
agent_relevance: A per-goal route store grows with the number of goals; our agent needs a cap and a ranking.

source: Kaelbling (1993) Learning to achieve goals, cited in Sagiv et al. as inspiration for the GR
finding: Goal-conditioned shortest-path learning for many goals at once is the ancestor of the GR. Seen only as a citation inside Sagiv et al.; the original paper was not read.
numbers: not read
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Same lineage as UVFA and HER: learn for all goals, not the current one.

source: Andrychowicz et al. (2017) Hindsight Experience Replay (NeurIPS)
finding: HER replays each episode with a different goal (one actually achieved) so a sparse-reward failure becomes a success for another goal. Closest engineering twin of goal-general replay.
numbers: Robot arm pushing, sliding, pick-and-place. Goal sampling strategy 'future' with k=4 or 8 worked best; 'final', 'episode', 'random' were worse. A pick-and-place policy trained in simulation ran on a real Fetch robot without fine-tuning.
quote: the most valuable goals for replay are the ones which are going to be achieved in the near future
limits: Needs a mapping from state to goal space; goals near the ones achieved soon after were the most useful, replaying goals far from them did no better.
agent_relevance: Relabeling failed runs with the goal they did reach is cheap goal-general memory. The 'future' rule suggests rehearsing goals likely to come soon, as in Sagiv.

source: Schaul, Quan, Antonoglou, Silver (2016) Prioritized Experience Replay (ICLR)
finding: Replay transitions in order of TD error instead of uniformly. The machine-learning form of the value-priority rule that Mattar and Daw later tied to hippocampal replay.
numbers: DQN with prioritized replay beat DQN with uniform replay on 41 of 49 Atari games. An oracle ordering on the Blind Cliffwalk gave exponential speed-ups over uniform replay.
limits: Priority tied to one value function and one task; can lose diversity. This is the 'value' side of the map-versus-value contrast.
agent_relevance: Plain error-priority memory chases the current task. Sagiv's point is that this can starve routes to goals not yet pursued.

source: Lampinen, Engelcke, Li, Chaudhry, McClelland (2025) Latent learning: episodic memory complements parametric learning by enabling flexible reuse of experiences
finding: Language models and agents fail at latent learning: using information seen in training but not needed for the training task (the Tolman rat result). Gridworld version: 20 objects per maze, 15 used as navigation targets in training, 5 held out as latent. Agents pass the held-out objects many times but do not learn routes to them.
numbers: Latent-object success stays far below trained-object success for both behavioral-cloning (ASCII tokens) and RL (pixels) baselines. Adding oracle episodic retrieval raised latent-object success significantly in both. On codebook and reversal text tests the no-retrieval baselines scored about 6 and 12 percent on the latent items.
quote: one weakness of parametric machine learning systems is their failure to exhibit latent learning
limits: Oracle retrieval, not a learned one. Benefit is muted where similarity cues exist or where training has few in-context-learning examples. Gridworld baselines can partly succeed by exploring.
agent_relevance: Direct machine test of 'map, not only value': an agent that keeps only goal-relevant data cannot reuse it. Keep raw episodes and retrieve them for new goals.

source: Lampinen et al. (2025) Latent learning, discussion of online versus offline replay
finding: Names two fixes: retrieve at test time, or replay ahead of time (preplay) to cache routes to alternative goals. Training-time replay costs compute at learning time but avoids a retrieval step, yet needs a guess of which goals will matter. Retrieval is more flexible.
numbers: No numbers; cites Carvalho et al. 2025 Multitask Preplay.
quote: these approaches also require estimating ahead of time which alternative goals may be relevant for future use; retrieval is more flexible
limits: Argues the two complement each other; no direct comparison run.
agent_relevance: Matches our design choice: precompute routes for likely goals (preplay) and keep a retrieval path for unexpected ones.

source: Carvalho, Hall-McMaster, Lee, Gershman (2025, v2 2026) Preemptive Solving of Future Problems: Multitask Preplay in Humans and Machines
finding: Multitask Preplay replays experience on one task as the start of counterfactual simulation of accessible but unpursued tasks, learning a predictive representation. Humans reuse prior paths for new goals more than planners predict, and the model reproduces this.
numbers: Human exp 1 (n=100): partial path reuse 62.39% (95% CI 53.99-69.53) vs 50% chance, p=0.0049. Exp 2 (shortcut opens): reuse 62.80%, p<.001. Another experiment: 67.1% and 67.3% in two conditions. Baselines in exp 2: Universal Value Functions 0% success, Universal Landmark SFs 7.65%, HER 5.56%; depth-first search reuse 39.00%, breadth-first 0%. Multitask Preplay: success 97.74%, reuse 99.50% (exp 2). Later experiment: HER 8.22%, Preplay 97.5% success and 99.3% reuse. First response time faster on reused paths (beta=-0.21, p=0.005).
limits: Reuse measured by two criteria (about 63% vs about 70%); intervals overlap. Gridworlds and 2D Minecraft only. Model reuses paths far more than people do (99% vs about 63%).
agent_relevance: Closest published test of Sagiv's idea in a deep-RL agent: goal-general methods (UVF, HER) fail where preplay of unpursued tasks works. Our agent should simulate nearby unpursued goals while idle.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in Large Language Models with CogEval
finding: Eight LLMs (nine columns in the score table) tested on tasks adapted from human cognitive-map experiments: multi-step paths, reward and transition revaluation, shortcut, detour. Models look competent on easy graphs but hallucinate invalid trajectories and loop. No out-of-the-box cognitive map.
numbers: GPT-4 table scores (mean): 1-step path 0.99; 2-step 0.82; 3-step 0.55; n-step 0.47; detour 0.55; shortcut 0.56; policy revaluation 0.21; reward revaluation 0.67; transition revaluation 0.60. Others lower (llama-13b 3-step 0.04, Bard n-step 0.00). 30 samples per prompt at temperatures 0, 0.5, 1 for OpenAI models.
limits: Temperature had no significant effect (F=1.28). Larger graphs were worse, and not only because of size. Text-only prompts.
agent_relevance: Quantifies the gap: LLMs do not hold a goal-general map. Policy revaluation (changed goal) is the weakest, the exact case a GR-style store is meant to fix.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval, Experiment 2: chain-of-thought and BFS/DFS instructions
finding: Adding chain-of-thought with BFS or DFS instructions helped only marginally and unevenly across models and task variants.
numbers: nonteleShortcutCoT: GPT-4 1.00 (SD 0.00), GPT-3.5 1.00, davinci-003 0.09, Claude-v1 0.58. teleShortcutCoT: GPT-4 0.50, davinci-003 0.04, llama-13b 0.83.
limits: SD of 0.00 suggests few scored items; benefit is not general.
agent_relevance: Prompting a search procedure is not a stable substitute for a stored map; give the agent an explicit graph to read.

source: Kim, Lee, Park, Seo (2024) How Language Models Extrapolate Outside the Training Data: A Case Study in Textualized Gridworld
finding: Fine-tuned LMs fail to extrapolate path planning to larger unseen mazes with next-token or plain CoT training. A cognitive-map chain of thought (build and mark a map, then plan on it) extrapolates, but needs special training and cannot be induced by simple prompting.
numbers: Optimal planning: no-CoT 19.0%, backward CoT 26.5%, cognitive map with backward unmark 76.5%. Reachable planning: none 32.1%, forward CoT 33.9%, cognitive map with backward mark 88.5%. Above 40% success at complexity 25 when training max was 15. DFS exploration reaches 94.5% reachability vs 88.5% for the cognitive map. Few-shot prompting reached up to 38%.
limits: Small fine-tuned models on gridworld text. Cognitive map needed training, not just a prompt. Exploration beats the map on reachability.
agent_relevance: Writing the map into the thought, instead of a bare path, gave large gains; a map-writing step is worth putting in the schema.

source: Dzhivelikian and Panov (2025) A biologically interpretable cognitive architecture for online structuring of episodic memories into cognitive maps
finding: Hebbian-like memory that merges episodic clusters using successor-feature similarity builds a map online in a partially observable 10x10 colored grid. Merging by successor features beats random merging and no merging.
numbers: Grid with 10 colors, episodes of 50 steps, 5 seeds x 3 colorings. Clusters of size 10 raise prediction accuracy above first-level and naive memory; too-large clusters fall to naive-model level; SF-based merging gives higher final accuracy than random.
limits: Small synthetic grid; no LLM; no replay prioritization by goal.
agent_relevance: A cheap rule exists for grouping episodes into a map: merge states with similar successor features.

source: Whittington, McCaffary, Bedford, Behrens (2022) Relating transformers to models and neural representations of the hippocampal formation (ICLR)
finding: Transformers with recurrent position encodings reproduce the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine and learn grid-like and place-like units. A formal bridge from hippocampal map models to the architecture LLMs use.
numbers: TEM-transformer learns grid-like representations (linear and ReLU variants) and memory neurons that remap randomly between environments like place cells.
limits: Small spatial tasks; shows representational similarity, not planning use. Not a test of replay.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that transformers can hold a map in principle, though it does not show a prompted LLM does.

source: Gutierrez, Shu, Gu, Yasunaga, Su (2024) HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
finding: Builds a knowledge graph (hippocampal index) from passages and runs Personalized PageRank from query concepts to retrieve linked passages in one step. A graph-spreading method from neuroscience used inside an LLM memory.
numbers: Average R@2/R@5 over MuSiQue, 2Wiki, HotpotQA: HippoRAG (ColBERTv2) 57.4/72.9. On 2Wiki, +11 points R@2 and +20 points R@5 over the best baseline; about +3 on MuSiQue; HotpotQA competitive. 10-30 times cheaper and 6-13 times faster than IRCoT. Combined with IRCoT, up to +4% (MuSiQue) and +20% (2Wiki).
limits: A map of facts, not of action routes; no replay or goal weighting. Two hyperparameters tuned on 100 MuSiQue examples.
agent_relevance: A concrete way to get a map-like store from text that reaches multi-hop answers without iterating, but it is not goal-weighted.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows (routines) from past successful trajectories and conditions future runs on them. A route store keyed to task types, learned online or offline.
numbers: Relative success +51.1% over the autonomous baseline on WebArena (+12.0 absolute points over BrowserGym); +24.6% relative step success on Mind2Web cross-task; +7.6% to +7.9% over a method using human-written workflows.
limits: Workflows come from successes only; no weighting by likelihood of future goals. Agents sometimes ignore newly added actions (18.5% of tasks).
agent_relevance: Practical form of a route library. Adding Sagiv-style priority (keep routes by expected future use) is the missing step.

source: Ding (2026) AgentHER: Hindsight Experience Replay for LLM Agent Trajectory Relabeling
finding: Ports HER to language agents: a failed trajectory for goal A is relabeled by an LLM as a correct demonstration for an achievable goal B, then used for SFT or DPO. Four-stage pipeline with confidence gating.
numbers: WebArena and ToolBench, task-disjoint held-out. +7.6 to +11.4 points over success-only SFT across GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-72B/7B, LLaMA3.1-8B; +3.0 to +6.2 over Agent Workflow Memory; 2x sample efficiency. Naive random relabeling hurt by 6.1 points. Multi-judge check cut label noise 5.9% to 2.9%; human-rated precision 97.1% (WebArena), 96.0% (ToolBench). Cost $2.98 and 26 minutes for 3,000 trajectories.
limits: Training-time, not in-context. Needs relabel quality control. Gains largest on incomplete (+11.0/12.7) and constraint-violation failures; smallest for crashes (+2.0/1.8).
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM-agent use of goal-general replay. Relabeling to reached goals works only with verification; the naive version is harmful.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agent stores verbal self-reflections in an episodic buffer and reuses them on retry. A value-style memory tied to the current task: the contrast case for map memory.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. Gains over baselines: +22% absolute on ALFWorld in 12 steps, +20% on HotPotQA, up to +11% on HumanEval.
limits: Reflections target the failed task; transfer to other goals is not tested in the paper. A hallucination rate of 22% persisted in one ALFWorld analysis.
agent_relevance: Good for fixing the present task; does not by itself build routes for future goals.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI)
finding: Agent extracts natural-language insights from success and failure pairs and retrieves past successes; insights transfer to a new task family without weight updates.
numbers: Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER success rate: ExpeL retrieve-only 40.3 to 54.4% over four rounds; ExpeL+Reflexion 54.5 to 60.4%; ExpeL Transfer 59.0 to 64.2%. ExpeL matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at R3 vs 39%) and is below it on ALFWorld (54% vs 59%).
limits: Table was read from a two-column layout; row labels may be slightly off. Insights are general lessons, not goal-conditioned routes.
agent_relevance: Distilled cross-task insights help new tasks, a partial analog of keeping routes for future goals.

source: Yu et al. (2025) Dyna-Think: Synergizing Reasoning, Acting, and World Model Simulation in AI Agents
finding: Dyna-style training for LLM agents: first train a world model (next-state prediction and critique), then train the policy. Matches R1 best-of-n with half the tokens.
numbers: Avg success (a benchmark table, likely WindowsAgentArena): Qwen-32B 23.9, R1 26.9, DIT(R1) 26.9, +RFT 28.4, +vanilla Dyna 20.9, +DDT next-state 34.9, +DDT critique 32.8. About 2x fewer tokens than R1 (685B) at similar best-of-n. World-model accuracy +16.8 points absolute after training.
limits: Benchmark of the table not confirmed from layout. Simulates the chosen action, not goal-general maps. Vanilla Dyna hurt (20.9 vs 26.9).
agent_relevance: Offline simulation helps only if the world model is trained well; a poor simulator hurts. Relevant to any in-context 'imagine routes' step.

source: Yu et al. (2025) Dyna-Mind: Learning to Simulate from Experience for Better AI Agents
finding: ReSim teaches agents to reason with search trees built from real experience (vicarious trial and error); Dyna-GRPO adds online RL. Replays real rollouts as imagined futures.
numbers: ReSim: Sokoban 96.4% success; ALFWorld 87.7% success, above other methods tested. R1 also near-perfect on Sokoban but not on ALFWorld.
limits: Search trees come from the real environment, so faithful but costly; trained, not prompted. AndroidWorld numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Simulation grounded in stored real experience beat unaided reasoning on ALFWorld.

source: Holt, Pouplin, Ruiz Luyten, van der Schaar (2026) Fact-Augmented Lookahead Planning for LLM Agents (LWM-Planner, AISTATS)
finding: In-context Dyna: after each episode the agent extracts atomic facts (for example where the holes are), filters them, and uses them to simulate and look ahead. Improves over ReAct and Reflexion with no weight updates.
numbers: Highest normalised cumulative return across TextFrozenLake sizes, CrafterMini and ALFWorld (134 eval tasks, single seed); other baselines degrade as the state-action space grows while LWM-Planner keeps solving. Exact table values not recorded.
limits: Few seeds (three in most runs; ALFWorld single seed).
agent_relevance: A prompt-only way to store a map from experience and plan on it. Closest in-context analog to Dyna-SR.

source: Li et al. (2026, ICLR) Spinning Straw into Gold: Relabeling LLM Agent Trajectories in Hindsight for Successful Demonstrations (search snippet only)
finding: Relabels each completed trajectory with all goals it achieved and fine-tunes on them. Search snippet says it beats baselines on ALFWorld with one quarter of the ground-truth demonstrations; also tested on PlanCraft and WebShop.
numbers: from snippet only; no exact deltas read
limits: Not opened; numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Second independent hindsight-relabeling result for LLM agents; check before relying on it.

source: Stower et al. (2025) Multi-modal cognitive maps for language and vision based on neural successor representations (Neurocomputing; search snippet only)
finding: Neural successor-representation network models place-cell-like dynamics and cognitive maps over space and language inputs.
numbers: not read
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows SR maps can be learned over language input, a small step toward non-spatial maps.

source: Momennejad group (2025) Modular Agentic Planner (MAP), brain-inspired LLM planning (index page only)
finding: Modular LLM planner with components modeled on prefrontal planning; simulations touch the successor representation.
numbers: not read
limits: Only an index page appeared; paper not located or opened.
agent_relevance: Possible next read for a brain-inspired LLM planner.

source: Gap note: no study found testing Sagiv et al. GR prioritization in an LLM agent
url: (searches: WebSearch x5, arXiv API 429, Semantic Scholar empty, OpenAlex budget exhausted)
finding: As of Nov 2026 I found no LLM paper that implements goal-distribution-weighted replay. Nearest: HER-style relabeling (AgentHER), Multitask Preplay (deep RL), retrieval for latent learning (Lampinen), workflow stores (AWM).
numbers: none
limits: Search coverage limited by rate limits; absence is not proof.
agent_relevance: Open gap: rank stored routes by expected future-goal frequency and compare with recency or error ranking.
